what: Ormat Technologies develops geothermal power. It finds underground heat, drills wells, builds power plants that use that heat to generate electricity continuously, and sells the power under long contracts. It also manufactures the specialised equipment for these plants and operates battery storage projects.
customers: Electric utilities buying power under long-term agreements, mostly in the United States, Kenya, Guatemala and Indonesia, plus other developers who buy its power plant equipment.
money: Power sold from its own geothermal and solar plants under long-term contracts.
Geothermal power plant equipment manufactured for third-party developers.
Battery storage projects providing grid services.
moat: Geothermal is the only renewable source that generates continuously, day and night, regardless of weather — which makes it far more valuable to a grid than solar or wind. Ormat is one of very few companies that can find the resource, drill it, build the plant and manufacture the equipment, and the geothermal fields it has proved are themselves scarce, long-lived assets.
risks: Free cash flow was about negative $235.6M, because building geothermal plants requires years of spending before any power is sold.
Debt of $2.7B against $147.4M of cash is heavy, and geothermal development is financed against future contracted revenue.
The shares trade at about 40.7 times earnings and 15.0 times EV/EBITDA, which is a full price.
Geothermal exploration carries genuine resource risk: wells can come in weaker than expected after substantial money has been spent.
Projects in Kenya, Guatemala and Indonesia carry political, currency and counterparty risk alongside the operational kind.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year, from $663.1M in 2021 to $989.5M in 2025, with trailing revenue of $1.2B.
Geothermal power runs continuously, which commands better contract prices than intermittent solar or wind.
Long-term power purchase agreements produce contracted, inflation-adjusted revenue for decades.
Proved geothermal fields are scarce assets with very long lives and almost no fuel cost.
Data centre demand for round-the-clock clean power is a new and well-funded buyer class for exactly this kind of generation.
watch: Megawatts under construction and coming online, plus contracted power prices. Current revenue reflects plants built years ago; the development pipeline describes the future.
view: Geothermal has one property that makes it fundamentally more valuable than other renewables, and it is worth stating precisely: it runs all the time. Solar produces when the sun shines and wind when the wind blows, and a grid needs power when neither is happening. Geothermal heat does not care about the weather or the hour, which means a geothermal plant provides what utilities actually need and what batteries only partially substitute for. That earns better contract prices, and it is the whole basis of Ormat’s position.

The reason geothermal is a small share of global generation despite that advantage is that it is hard. You have to find the underground heat, which involves exploration risk — wells come in weaker than hoped after substantial money has been spent. Then you drill, build a plant and connect it, which takes years of capital before a single kilowatt is sold. Ormat is one of very few companies that can do the whole chain, including manufacturing the equipment, and that integration is a genuine advantage.

The financial profile follows directly. Negative free cash flow of $236 million and $2.7 billion of debt are what a developer looks like mid-build, not evidence of a problem — the spending today produces contracted revenue for decades. But it does mean the company is permanently dependent on financing, and that rising interest rates hurt both the cost of building and the value of the contracted cash flows already owned.

The newer development that genuinely improves the outlook is data centre demand. Technology companies want clean power available around the clock, and that is an extremely short list of options: nuclear, hydro and geothermal. Having well-funded buyers competing for continuously available clean electricity is a better position than Ormat has ever had. At 40.7 times earnings and 15 times EV/EBITDA, the price already reflects some of this; what justifies holding is megawatts under construction and the prices being contracted, not this year’s income statement.
bull: Data centres and utilities compete for round-the-clock clean power, contracted prices rise, and the development pipeline converts years of spending into decades of revenue.
bear: Exploration wells disappoint, high rates raise financing costs against $2.7 billion of debt, and emerging-market counterparties fail to pay on long contracts.
